title: How to Read Types and Shadows Without Going Off the Rails
subtitle: A disciplined guide to biblical typology, how to recognize legitimate types and shadows in the Old Testament, and how to avoid allegory and fanciful interpretation

sections.title: The Promise and the Peril of Typology
sections.body:
Typology is one of the richest ways to read the Old Testament and one of the easiest to wreck. It is the recognition that God built patterns into history, persons and events and institutions that foreshadow a greater reality to come, above all Christ himself.

The peril is that once a reader starts finding patterns, he can find them everywhere, including where God put none.

There are two ditches on this road. In one ditch sits the reader so afraid of excess that he refuses to see the types the New Testament plainly names. In the other sits the reader who sees the cross in every scarlet thread and the Trinity in every set of three, spinning meanings the text never carried. The first man starves. The second man hallucinates. The discipline of typology is the narrow road between them, and it is walkable, but only if you hold the rules.

sections.title: What a Type Actually Is
sections.body:
A type is a real person, event, or institution in the Old Testament that God designed to prefigure a greater fulfillment, called the antitype, in the New. The key word is real. Adam was a real man. The Passover lamb was a real lamb. The bronze serpent was a real pole in a real wilderness. Typology does not dissolve the history. It honors it and then sees beyond it.

This is what separates typology from allegory. Allegory treats the surface story as a code to be cracked, where the details secretly stand for something else and the history barely matters. Typology lets the history stand and traces the pattern God laid through it.

So a type has two marks. It is grounded in genuine history, and it points forward by genuine design to a greater fulfillment in Christ and his work. Lose the first and you have fiction. Lose the second and you have only an old story. Hold both and you have a type.

sections.title: The Rules That Keep You on the Rails
sections.body:
Here are the guardrails. Cross them and you are no longer interpreting. You are inventing.

First, let the New Testament teach you what types look like before you go hunting for your own. Scripture names many of them outright. Adam as a type of Christ. The Passover lamb. The bronze serpent. Melchizedek. Learn the pattern from the clear cases the apostles gave you.

Second, a type must rest on a real correspondence God built in, not a clever resemblance you noticed. The fact that something is red does not make it the blood of Christ. Third, look for escalation: the antitype is always greater than the type, the reality larger than the shadow. Fourth, the meaning you draw must agree with the plain doctrine taught elsewhere, never contradict it or float free of it. A type confirms the gospel. It does not smuggle in a new one. Keep these four and you will see what God put there without painting in things he did not.

sections.title: What Off the Rails Looks Like
sections.body:
You have heard the bad fruit. The sermon that finds the cross in the two sticks the widow gathered. The teacher who turns every measurement of the tabernacle into a hidden prophecy. The whole study that makes the colors of the priestly garments into a secret system of doctrine.

This is not depth. It is the imagination wearing the Bible as a costume.

The damage is real and runs two ways. It trains people to think Scripture is a puzzle box that only the initiated can open, which strips the ordinary believer of his confidence to read. And it severs interpretation from control, so that the cleverest guesser wins and the text loses its authority entirely. I have sat under that kind of teaching and felt the strange thrill of it, and only later understood that I had learned nothing about God and a great deal about the speaker's ingenuity. Cleverness is not the goal. Faithfulness is. The type was God's idea before it was your discovery.

sections.title: The Reward of the Disciplined Eye
sections.body:
Do this with discipline and the Old Testament comes alive in a way that moralizing never delivers. You begin to see the design, the long preparation, the God who was telling one story all along.

The sacrificial system stops being a strange catalog of slaughter and becomes a centuries long lesson teaching a people that sin costs blood, so that when John points and says behold the Lamb of God, the whole nation has been schooled to understand him. The exodus stops being only ancient politics and becomes the pattern of every rescue God works, including the one he worked on you.

This is the reward, and it is given to the patient, not the clever. See only what God built. Trace only the patterns he laid. Let every shadow point to its substance and then get out of the way. The disciplined eye does not find less in the Old Testament. It finds the Christ who was there the whole time, and it does not have to lie to find him.
